examples: Sit here next to me.
Is Anna here today?
It's really cold in here.

senses.head: To this place

How long did it take you to get here?

senses.head: At this point in a process, discussion or piece of writing; in this matter or situation
body: (в этом месте, на этом этапе, в данном случае)
examples: Let's stop here for today.
Here the author changes her argument.
The real problem here is the cost.

senses.head: Used to present, offer or point out something, or to say that someone or something has arrived
examples: Here are your keys.
Here comes the bus.
Here you go — one coffee, no sugar.

senses.head: Used when raising a glass to someone in a toast
examples: Here's to the happy couple!

entries.position: end — or front with inversion: Here comes the bus
entries.modifies: verbs; also follows a noun (the people here)
entries.contrast: Russian has two words, здесь (where?) and сюда (where to?); English uses here for both, with no preposition: Come here, never come to here. In the presenting use a noun subject comes after the verb (Here comes the bus, Here are your keys), but a pronoun does not (Here it comes, Here they are).

My sister was always there for me.
Whatever happens, I'll be there for you.

The demand is clearly there, so why not open a second store?

senses.head: In or at that place
examples: I left my bag over there.
Were you there when it happened?
Put the boxes down there, by the door.

senses.head: To that place
examples: We drove there in two hours.
I've never been there, but I'd love to go.
Wait for me — I'll be there in five minutes.

senses.head: At that point in a process, discussion or story; in that respect
examples: I'll stop there and take questions.
There I have to disagree with you.
The story could have ended there, but it didn't.

senses.head: Used to point out or draw attention to someone or something, or to show that you have found them
examples: There goes the last train.
There you are — I've been looking everywhere for you.
There she is — right on time.

senses.head: Used after a greeting or to call someone's attention
examples: Hi there! How's it going?
Hello there — can I help you find something?

senses.head: Available to help and support someone, especially emotionally
examples: My sister was always there for me.
Whatever happens, I'll be there for you.

senses.head: Existing or available, even if not yet used or noticed
examples: The talent is there — he just needs to work harder.
The money is there if we need it.
The demand is clearly there, so why not open a second store?

senses.head: At the goal or the result that you want; succeeding
examples: The design isn't quite there yet.
It took years of practice, but she finally got there.

entries.position: end — or front with inversion: There goes the last train
entries.modifies: verbs; also follows a noun (that man there)
entries.contrast: The there of there is / there are is a dummy subject, not this adverb, and does not mean там: There is a pharmacy there uses both. Like here, it covers both там and туда with no preposition: go there, never go to there. With a noun subject the verb comes first (There goes my bus), with a pronoun it does not (There it goes). Do not confuse it with their and they're, which sound the same.

entries.meaning: In, at or to every place. ---
examples: I've looked everywhere for my glasses.
There were people everywhere downtown.
My little brother follows me everywhere.
entries.position: end — or front for emphasis
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.form: every + where, like somewhere, anywhere, nowhere
entries.contrast: Not everywhere means не везде (only some places). For нигде after a negative verb use anywhere: I can't find it anywhere, not everywhere. Before a clause it works as a conjunction meaning wherever: Everywhere we went, people were friendly.

examples: My keys were nowhere to be found.
Nowhere in the contract does it mention overtime.
The kids were nowhere in sight.
After the fire, the family had nowhere else to go.
I'm going nowhere until you tell me the truth.
We talked for hours and got nowhere.
This relationship is going nowhere.
Without my first coach, I'd be nowhere today.
The report is nowhere near finished.
The sequel is nowhere near as good as the original.
We have nowhere near enough chairs.

senses.head: Not in or at any place
examples: My keys were nowhere to be found.
Nowhere in the contract does it mention overtime.
The kids were nowhere in sight.

senses.head: Not to any place
examples: After the fire, the family had nowhere else to go.
I'm going nowhere until you tell me the truth.

senses.head: To no progress, result or success, especially with get, go or be
body: (ни к чему (не привести), ни с места, ничего не добиться)
examples: We talked for hours and got nowhere.
This relationship is going nowhere.
Without my first coach, I'd be nowhere today.

senses.head: In nowhere near: not at all; far from
examples: The report is nowhere near finished.
The sequel is nowhere near as good as the original.
We have nowhere near enough chairs.

entries.type: place; also direction, negative and degree
entries.position: end — front only with inversion: Nowhere is this clearer than…
entries.modifies: verbs; nowhere near modifies adjectives, numbers and phrases
entries.form: no + where; the negative of somewhere and anywhere
entries.contrast: English allows one negative per clause. Russian Я никуда не иду is I'm not going anywhere or I'm going nowhere, never I'm not going nowhere. Fronted, it forces inversion: Nowhere have I seen such beautiful beaches. The middle of nowhere and out of nowhere use nowhere as a noun.

examples: I left my phone somewhere in the car.
Let's sit somewhere quiet.
He lives somewhere near Boston.
Are you going somewhere?
Let's go somewhere warm this winter.
She's somewhere around fifty.
We got home somewhere around midnight.
A good laptop costs somewhere between $800 and $1,200.
Now we're getting somewhere!
After three meetings we finally got somewhere on the budget.

senses.head: In or at a place that is not known or not named
examples: I left my phone somewhere in the car.
Let's sit somewhere quiet.
He lives somewhere near Boston.

senses.head: To a place that is not known or not named
examples: Are you going somewhere?
Let's go somewhere warm this winter.

senses.head: About; approximately, with a number, a time or a range
examples: She's somewhere around fifty.
We got home somewhere around midnight.
A good laptop costs somewhere between $800 and $1,200.

senses.head: In get somewhere: to make progress
examples: Now we're getting somewhere!
After three meetings we finally got somewhere on the budget.

entries.position: end — before a number or time in the approximate sense: somewhere around fifty
entries.modifies: verbs; numbers after around or between
entries.form: some + where; American informal someplace means the same
entries.contrast: Use somewhere in statements, and in offers and requests that expect yes (Would you like to go somewhere?); use anywhere in negatives and most questions (I didn't go anywhere). An adjective follows it: somewhere quiet, not quiet somewhere.

examples: I can't find my keys anywhere.
Did you go anywhere last weekend?
Is there a pharmacy anywhere near here?
Sit anywhere you like.
You can buy these batteries anywhere.
I'd go anywhere with you.
The drive takes anywhere from three to five hours.
Tickets cost anywhere between $50 and $500.
I'm not anywhere near ready.
The new stadium isn't anywhere near as big as the old one.
Arguing with him won't get you anywhere.
Are we getting anywhere with this plan?

senses.head: In negatives and questions: in, at or to any place
examples: I can't find my keys anywhere.
Did you go anywhere last weekend?
Is there a pharmacy anywhere near here?

senses.head: In or to any place at all; it does not matter where
examples: Sit anywhere you like.
You can buy these batteries anywhere.
I'd go anywhere with you.

senses.head: Any amount within a range, with from … to or between
examples: The drive takes anywhere from three to five hours.
Tickets cost anywhere between $50 and $500.

senses.head: In not anywhere near: not at all; far from
examples: I'm not anywhere near ready.
The new stadium isn't anywhere near as big as the old one.

senses.head: In negatives and questions with get: to any progress or result
examples: Arguing with him won't get you anywhere.
Are we getting anywhere with this plan?

entries.position: end — before a number in the range sense: anywhere from three to five hours
entries.modifies: verbs; numbers after from or between
entries.form: any + where; American informal anyplace means the same
entries.contrast: In a statement anywhere means где угодно (any place at all), not где-то: I left it somewhere, not I left it anywhere. After a negative verb it gives нигде / никуда: I can't find it anywhere. Do not add a second negative (not … nowhere).

entries.meaning: In, at or to another place or other places. ---
examples: If you don't like the prices, shop elsewhere.
Elsewhere in the state, rents are much lower.
As I mentioned elsewhere in the report, costs are rising.
entries.русский: в другом месте, в другое место
entries.position: end — or front, especially in news: Elsewhere, stocks fell; also after a noun: people elsewhere
entries.modifies: verbs; also follows a noun
entries.contrast: Elsewhere is a little more formal than somewhere else; in negatives and questions everyday speech uses anywhere else: We couldn't find it anywhere else.

examples: My office is upstairs.
The kids are playing upstairs.
We can hear the neighbors upstairs every night.
She ran upstairs to get her coat.
Can you take these bags upstairs?

senses.head: On a higher floor of a building
examples: My office is upstairs.
The kids are playing upstairs.
We can hear the neighbors upstairs every night.

senses.head: Up the stairs to a higher floor
examples: She ran upstairs to get her coat.
Can you take these bags upstairs?

entries.position: end — or after a noun: the neighbors upstairs
entries.modifies: verbs; also follows a noun
entries.form: up + stairs; the final -s belongs to the adverb, it is not a plural
entries.contrast: No preposition after a verb of motion: go upstairs, not go to upstairs. Before a noun it is an adjective, stressed on the first syllable (the UPstairs bathroom).

examples: Breakfast is served downstairs.
I'll wait for you downstairs in the lobby.
The people downstairs complained about the noise.
He hurried downstairs to answer the door.
Carry the laundry downstairs for me, please.

senses.head: On a lower floor of a building, especially the ground floor
examples: Breakfast is served downstairs.
I'll wait for you downstairs in the lobby.
The people downstairs complained about the noise.

senses.head: Down the stairs to a lower floor
examples: He hurried downstairs to answer the door.
Carry the laundry downstairs for me, please.

entries.position: end — or after a noun: the apartment downstairs
entries.modifies: verbs; also follows a noun
entries.form: down + stairs; the final -s belongs to the adverb, it is not a plural
entries.contrast: No preposition after a verb of motion: come downstairs, not come to downstairs. Before a noun it is an adjective, stressed on the first syllable (a DOWNstairs bedroom).

The kids are playing outside.

senses.head: Not in a building; in the open air
examples: It's freezing outside.
The kids are playing outside.
Let's eat outside tonight.

senses.head: Out of a building or room, to the outside
examples: Could you step outside for a minute?
I'll take the dog outside.

senses.head: On the outer side or surface of something
examples: The house looks old outside, but it's modern inside.
We're having the house painted outside this summer.

entries.position: end — or front: Outside, it was snowing
entries.modifies: verbs; also follows a noun (the noise outside)
entries.contrast: Russian на улице about weather or being out of the house is outside, not on the street: It's cold outside, The kids are playing outside. With an object it is a preposition (outside the house); American English also says outside of the house.

senses.head: In a building, room or container
examples: Let's wait inside until the rain stops.
It's much warmer inside.
The box had a note inside.

senses.head: Into a building, room or container
examples: Come inside — it's getting dark.
She opened the envelope and looked inside.

senses.head: In your mind or feelings, often hidden from others
examples: She smiled, but inside she was furious.
After the breakup, I felt empty inside.

entries.position: end — front for the feelings sense: Inside, she was furious
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.contrast: With an object it is a preposition (inside the car); American English also says inside of the car, and inside of an hour means within an hour. Inside out means наизнанку, not изнутри наружу.

senses.head: In a building rather than outside
examples: The kids stayed indoors all day because of the rain.
Smoking indoors is not allowed.

senses.head: Into a building
examples: We went indoors when it started to rain.
Bring the plants indoors before the first frost.

entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.form: in + doors; the adjective is indoor, with no -s
entries.contrast: The adverb ends in -s and the adjective does not: We played indoors but an indoor pool, never an indoors pool or played indoor.

examples: We ate outdoors on the patio.
He works outdoors all year round.
Let's take the kids outdoors for some fresh air.

senses.head: Outside a building; in the open air

He works outdoors all year round.

senses.head: Out of a building into the open air
examples: Let's take the kids outdoors for some fresh air.
When the rain stopped, we moved the party outdoors.

entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.form: out + doors; the adjective is outdoor, with no -s
entries.contrast: The adverb ends in -s and the adjective does not: We ate outdoors but an outdoor café. The great outdoors is a noun (природа, дикая местность).

examples: Do you live nearby?

entries.position: end — or after a noun: a café nearby
entries.modifies: verbs; also follows a noun
entries.form: near + by, written as one word
entries.contrast: With an object use near: near the school; nearby the school also occurs but is much less common and sounds awkward to many speakers. Before a noun it is an adjective (a nearby town); after a noun it is the adverb (a town nearby).

senses.head: In a foreign country
examples: She lived abroad for ten years.
Many students spend a semester studying abroad.

senses.head: To a foreign country
examples: We're going abroad this summer.
He moved abroad right after college.

senses.head: Formal: spreading widely among people; in circulation
examples: Rumors were abroad that the plant would close.

entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs; also follows a noun (news from abroad)
entries.contrast: No preposition before it after a verb: go abroad, live abroad, not go to abroad or in abroad (but from abroad is fine). Do not confuse it with aboard (на борту). In everyday American speech overseas is often used instead, though study abroad is the fixed phrase.

senses.head: In a foreign country, especially one across an ocean

The company makes most of its money overseas.

senses.head: To a foreign country across an ocean
examples: She moved overseas for a job in Tokyo.

entries.русский: за границей, за границу, за океаном
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.contrast: No preposition after a verb: go overseas, not go to overseas. Before a noun it is an adjective (overseas markets). Americans use it for almost any trip abroad except to Canada or Mexico.

entries.meaning: Above your head; in the sky. ---
examples: Planes flew overhead all night.
A hawk was circling overhead.
A single bulb swung overhead in the basement.
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.contrast: The adverb is stressed on the last syllable (planes flew overHEAD); the adjective and noun are stressed on the first (OVERhead bin, OVERhead costs). The noun overhead means накладные расходы.

senses.head: Below the surface of the ground
examples: The power lines run underground.
Moles spend most of their lives underground.
The miners work almost a mile underground.

senses.head: In or into secret, hiding from the authorities
examples: The group went underground after it was banned.
He lived underground for years under a false name.

entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.contrast: The adverb is stressed on the last syllable; the adjective on the first (an UNderground garage). The Underground is the London subway — in the US say subway.

examples: She works downtown at a bank.
Parking downtown costs a fortune.
Let's take the train downtown.
We drove downtown for dinner and a show.

senses.head: In the center or main business district of a city
examples: She works downtown at a bank.
Parking downtown costs a fortune.

senses.head: To or toward the center of a city
examples: Let's take the train downtown.
We drove downtown for dinner and a show.

entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.contrast: An American word: downtown is the central business district, not the lower part of town (British English says in town or the city centre). No preposition after a verb: go downtown, not go to downtown — to downtown Chicago uses it as a noun. In Manhattan it also means the southern part.

examples: My grandparents live uptown.
The museum is uptown, near the park.
Take the express train uptown to 110th Street.
After the show, we headed uptown.

senses.head: In the part of a city away from the center, usually residential, or in New York the northern part
body: (в северной части города, в жилом районе)
examples: My grandparents live uptown.
The museum is uptown, near the park.

senses.head: To or toward that part of a city
examples: Take the express train uptown to 110th Street.
After the show, we headed uptown.

entries.русский: в северной части города, в жилые кварталы
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.contrast: An American word with no British equivalent: the part of a city away from downtown, usually residential, and in Manhattan the northern part. The adjective uptown can also mean upscale (an uptown restaurant). No preposition after a verb: go uptown.

examples: The road ahead is closed.

If you buy now, you'll come out ahead in the long run.
"Can I ask a question?" "Sure, go ahead."
Go ahead and start eating — don't wait for me.
The concert will go ahead despite the rain.

senses.head: In front; further forward in space
examples: The road ahead is closed.
There's a gas station a mile ahead.
Keep your eyes straight ahead.

senses.head: Forward, in the direction you are facing or going
examples: She ran ahead to get us a table.
The kids raced ahead down the trail.

senses.head: In or into the future
examples: We have a busy week ahead.
It's time to look ahead and make a plan.

senses.head: Before the time something happens; in advance
examples: Call ahead to reserve a table.
If you plan ahead, the move will be easy.

senses.head: Winning, leading, or in a better position than others
examples: Our team was ahead by ten points at halftime.
If you buy now, you'll come out ahead in the long run.

senses.head: In go ahead: to start or continue doing something; used to give permission
examples: "Can I ask a question?" "Sure, go ahead."
Go ahead and start eating — don't wait for me.
The concert will go ahead despite the rain.

entries.position: end — or after a noun: the road ahead
entries.comparison: not gradable — use further: further ahead
entries.modifies: verbs; also follows a noun (the road ahead)
entries.contrast: With an object it becomes ahead of (ahead of me, ahead of time). Go ahead usually means давай, пожалуйста (permission), not иди вперёд. For the direction of a single step say forward: step forward, not step ahead.

examples: She walked ahead, and I followed behind.
A police car was following close behind.
The rest of the hikers were a long way behind.
I left my wallet behind at the restaurant.
He stayed behind after class to help clean up.
He leaves behind a wife and two children.
I fell behind in chemistry after I got sick.
We're three months behind on the rent.
The Yankees were behind by two runs in the ninth.

senses.head: At or toward the back; following someone or something
examples: She walked ahead, and I followed behind.
A police car was following close behind.
The rest of the hikers were a long way behind.

senses.head: Remaining in the place you are leaving, or still there after someone has gone or died
examples: I left my wallet behind at the restaurant.
He stayed behind after class to help clean up.
He leaves behind a wife and two children.

senses.head: Late, slower than planned, or losing; not keeping up
examples: I fell behind in chemistry after I got sick.
We're three months behind on the rent.
The Yankees were behind by two runs in the ninth.

entries.position: end
entries.comparison: not gradable — use further: further behind
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.contrast: Russian speakers copy in front of and say behind of the house; the preposition is just behind the house, with no of. Stay behind means остаться (на месте), not отстать — that is fall behind. The noun behind is informal for зад, попа.

examples: The people in the apartment above are really loud.
Seen from above, the city looks like a map.
Dark clouds gathered above.
See the chart above for details.

Any grade of 90 or above is an A.
The order came from above.
She believed the help was sent from above.

senses.head: At or to a higher place; overhead
examples: The people in the apartment above are really loud.
Seen from above, the city looks like a map.
Dark clouds gathered above.

senses.head: Earlier in a piece of writing
examples: See the chart above for details.
As mentioned above, the deadline is Friday.

senses.head: More than a stated number, amount or level
examples: The class is for kids aged 12 and above.
Any grade of 90 or above is an A.

senses.head: In a higher position of authority, or in heaven
examples: The order came from above.
She believed the help was sent from above.

entries.position: end — or after a noun: the chart above
entries.modifies: verbs; follows a noun or a number
entries.contrast: For earlier text Russian says выше, but English says above, not higher: see above, the example above. With an object it is a preposition (above the door); the above (the above address) is a formal adjective or noun use.

examples: From the bridge we watched the river below.
The apartment below has been empty for months.
The pot fell to the sidewalk below.
See the table below.
Sign your name in the space below.
Anyone who scores 60 or below has to retake the test.
It was fifteen below in Minneapolis last night.
The captain ordered the passengers to go below.
Two sailors were sleeping below.

senses.head: At or to a lower place
examples: From the bridge we watched the river below.
The apartment below has been empty for months.
The pot fell to the sidewalk below.

senses.head: Later in a piece of writing
examples: See the table below.
Sign your name in the space below.

senses.head: Less than a stated number or level, including below zero on a thermometer
examples: Anyone who scores 60 or below has to retake the test.
It was fifteen below in Minneapolis last night.

senses.head: On or to a lower deck of a ship
examples: The captain ordered the passengers to go below.
Two sailors were sleeping below.

entries.position: end — or after a noun: the table below
entries.modifies: verbs; follows a noun or a number
entries.contrast: For later text say below, not lower: see below. In American weather talk ten below means ten degrees below zero Fahrenheit. With an object it is a preposition (below the window).

examples: They stood on the cliff and looked at the waves beneath.

entries.position: end — or after a noun: the valley beneath
entries.modifies: verbs; also follows a noun
entries.contrast: Mostly a preposition (beneath the bridge); the adverb is formal or literary, and everyday speech uses below or underneath. It's beneath me (ниже моего достоинства) is the preposition, not this adverb.

examples: I lifted the rug and found the keys underneath.
She wore a sweater with a T-shirt underneath.
The car looks fine but is rusting underneath.
He seems tough, but underneath he's very kind.
Underneath, she was terrified.

senses.head: Directly under something, or on its lower side
examples: I lifted the rug and found the keys underneath.
She wore a sweater with a T-shirt underneath.
The car looks fine but is rusting underneath.

senses.head: Behind the way someone looks or acts; in reality
examples: He seems tough, but underneath he's very kind.
Underneath, she was terrified.

entries.position: front or end — front for the hidden-feelings sense
entries.modifies: verbs; whole clauses in the second sense
entries.form: under + neath (an old word for below)
entries.contrast: With an object it is a preposition (underneath the bed). In the second sense it opens the clause and means в глубине души, not a physical place.

examples: I'm going home — I'm exhausted.

Push the cartridge home until it clicks.

senses.head: To the place where you live
examples: I'm going home — I'm exhausted.
What time did you get home last night?
Can you drive me home after the party?

senses.head: At the place where you live
examples: Is your dad home?
I stayed home all weekend.
Nobody's home right now.

senses.head: To or in your own country or hometown
examples: After ten years in Europe, she came home to Texas.
It's time to bring the troops home.

senses.head: So that something is fully felt or understood
examples: The reality of losing her job finally hit home.
The ad drives home the message that speeding kills.
Seeing his empty room really brought it home to me that he was gone.

senses.head: Fully into the right place, as far as it will go
examples: He hammered the nail home.
Push the cartridge home until it clicks.

entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs of motion, and be and stay
entries.contrast: After verbs of motion home takes no preposition: go home, get home, arrive home, never go to home or arrive to home. For location American English says both stay home and stay at home, Is Dad home? and Is Dad at home?; British English prefers at home. With a possessive it is a noun and needs the preposition: go to my home.

examples: Go away and leave me alone!
He turned and walked away without a word.
The bird flew away.

The nearest hospital is an hour away.
Stay away from the edge!

We'll be away until Monday.
She looked away when I smiled at her.
He turned away from the window.
Put your toys away before dinner.
They've been putting money away for college.
Don't throw that box away — I need it.
We gave most of our furniture away before the move.
The store is giving away free samples today.
The snow melted away by noon.
The music slowly faded away.
She was typing away at her laptop all night.
You have questions? Ask away.
Christmas is only two weeks away.
The election is still a year away.
I'll call you back right away.

senses.head: From a place; leaving or moving to a different place
examples: Go away and leave me alone!
He turned and walked away without a word.
The bird flew away.

senses.head: At a distance from someone or something, often a stated one
examples: The beach is only two miles away.
The nearest hospital is an hour away.
Stay away from the edge!

senses.head: Not at home or at work; out of town for a period of time
examples: She's away on business this week.
We'll be away until Monday.

senses.head: Turning in another direction
examples: She looked away when I smiled at her.
He turned away from the window.

senses.head: Into a safe or proper place, especially to store or save something
examples: Put your toys away before dinner.
They've been putting money away for college.

senses.head: So that you no longer have something; out of your possession
examples: Don't throw that box away — I need it.
We gave most of our furniture away before the move.
The store is giving away free samples today.

senses.head: So that something gets smaller and disappears
examples: The snow melted away by noon.
The music slowly faded away.

senses.head: Continuously and busily, without stopping
examples: She was typing away at her laptop all night.
You have questions? Ask away.

senses.head: In the future, at a stated distance in time
examples: Christmas is only two weeks away.
The election is still a year away.

senses.head: In right away: immediately
examples: I'll call you back right away.
She knew right away that something was wrong.

entries.type: place; also direction, time and particle
entries.position: end
entries.comparison: not gradable — use farther or further: farther away
entries.modifies: verbs; follows a distance or a length of time (two miles away)
entries.contrast: Distance and time go before away: The station is five minutes away, never five minutes far or far in five minutes. She's out means she has left for a short time; she's away means she is traveling for days. Way in way too expensive is a separate informal degree adverb. In phrasal verbs (throw away, give away, put away) it is a particle whose meaning is part of the verb.

examples: The two towns are ten miles apart.
Our birthdays are just three days apart.
Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
My parents have lived apart for years.
The twins had never spent a night apart.
The old book fell apart in my hands.
He took the engine apart to fix it.
Her voice sets her apart from other singers.
He always kept himself apart from the other kids.

senses.head: Separated by a stated distance or time
body: (на расстоянии (друг от друга), с разницей в)
examples: The two towns are ten miles apart.
Our birthdays are just three days apart.
Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.

senses.head: Not together; separately
examples: My parents have lived apart for years.
The twins had never spent a night apart.

senses.head: Into pieces
examples: The old book fell apart in my hands.
He took the engine apart to fix it.

senses.head: Different from or kept separate from others
examples: Her voice sets her apart from other singers.
He always kept himself apart from the other kids.

entries.position: end
entries.comparison: not gradable — use farther or further: farther apart
entries.modifies: verbs; follows a distance or a length of time (three days apart)
entries.contrast: Apart (one word) means separated; a part (two words) means часть: She is a part of the team vs They live apart. Apart from is a preposition meaning кроме (American English also says aside from).

examples: She stepped aside to let me pass.
He pushed his plate aside and stood up.
Can I take you aside for a minute?
I put aside $50 a week for vacation.
Set aside an hour at the end for questions.
Jokes aside, we really need to talk.
Cost aside, it's a great idea.

senses.head: To one side; out of the way
examples: She stepped aside to let me pass.
He pushed his plate aside and stood up.
Can I take you aside for a minute?

senses.head: Saved or kept for later use
examples: I put aside $50 a week for vacation.
Set aside an hour at the end for questions.

senses.head: Not counted or considered for the moment, after a noun
examples: Jokes aside, we really need to talk.
Cost aside, it's a great idea.

entries.position: end — or after a noun: jokes aside
entries.modifies: verbs; follows a noun in the sense not counting
entries.contrast: Aside from is a preposition meaning кроме (the American form of apart from). Do not confuse it with beside (рядом с) or besides (кроме того). The noun an aside is a remark made in passing.

examples: The sailors rowed ashore at dawn.
Tons of plastic wash ashore every year.
The crew spent the night ashore.
Cruise passengers get four hours ashore in Nassau.

senses.head: From the water onto the land
examples: The sailors rowed ashore at dawn.
Tons of plastic wash ashore every year.

senses.head: On land, not on a ship
examples: The crew spent the night ashore.
Cruise passengers get four hours ashore in Nassau.

entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.form: a- + shore, like aboard and afloat
entries.contrast: No preposition after a verb: come ashore, not come to ashore. Like other a- words it never goes before a noun; say the crew on shore, not the ashore crew.

examples: There were 180 passengers aboard.
Is everyone aboard?
We climbed aboard just before the doors closed.
"All aboard!" the conductor shouted.
Welcome aboard — we're glad to have you.
We brought a new designer aboard last month.

senses.head: On a ship, plane, train or bus
examples: There were 180 passengers aboard.
Is everyone aboard?

senses.head: Onto a ship, plane, train or bus
examples: We climbed aboard just before the doors closed.
"All aboard!" the conductor shouted.

senses.head: Into a company, team or group as a new member
examples: Welcome aboard — we're glad to have you.
We brought a new designer aboard last month.

entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.contrast: Do not confuse aboard (на борту) with abroad (за границей). With an object it is a preposition and takes no of: aboard the ship. On board means the same and is more common in speech.

examples: The ship anchored a mile offshore.
Much of the oil is now drilled offshore.
The wind was blowing offshore.
A strong current pulled the swimmer offshore.
The company moved thousands of jobs offshore.
He kept most of his money offshore.

senses.head: At sea, some distance from the coast
examples: The ship anchored a mile offshore.
Much of the oil is now drilled offshore.

senses.head: Away from the land and toward the sea
examples: The wind was blowing offshore.
A strong current pulled the swimmer offshore.

senses.head: In or to another country, especially to pay lower taxes or wages
examples: The company moved thousands of jobs offshore.
He kept most of his money offshore.

entries.русский: в море, вдали от берега; за рубежом
entries.position: end
entries.modifies: verbs
entries.form: off + shore; the opposite is onshore
entries.contrast: Russian офшор is a noun; English offshore is an adjective or adverb, so say an offshore company or an offshore account, not an offshore. Do not confuse it with ashore (на берег), which means the opposite direction.

examples: The town is about fifty miles inland.
It's much hotter inland in the summer.
The hurricane moved inland overnight.
The settlers traveled inland along the river.

senses.head: In an area away from the coast
examples: The town is about fifty miles inland.
It's much hotter inland in the summer.

senses.head: Away from the coast toward the middle of a country
examples: The hurricane moved inland overnight.
The settlers traveled inland along the river.

entries.position: end
entries.comparison: not gradable — use further: further inland
entries.modifies: verbs; follows a distance (fifty miles inland)
entries.contrast: Russian внутренний about travel within a country is domestic, not inland: domestic flights. Inland is about distance from the sea or coast.

examples: The town lies midway between Denver and Salt Lake City.
We stopped midway for lunch.
He walked out midway through the movie.
Midway through the season, the coach was fired.

senses.head: In the middle of the distance between two places
examples: The town lies midway between Denver and Salt Lake City.
We stopped midway for lunch.

senses.head: In the middle of a period of time or an event
examples: He walked out midway through the movie.
Midway through the season, the coach was fired.

entries.position: front or end
entries.modifies: verbs; phrases with between and through
entries.contrast: In American English the midway is also a noun: the part of a fair with games and rides. Midway is a little more formal than halfway, and has no degree sense (halfway decent, not midway decent).

examples: We're halfway there — keep going.
She stopped halfway up the stairs.
The gas station is halfway between the two towns.
I fell asleep halfway through the movie.
We're about halfway done with the renovation.
I halfway believed his story.
Anything halfway decent in this neighborhood costs a fortune.
I can't pay $500, but I'll meet you halfway.
If both sides met halfway, the strike could end tomorrow.

senses.head: At or to the middle point between two places
examples: We're halfway there — keep going.
She stopped halfway up the stairs.
The gas station is halfway between the two towns.

senses.head: In the middle of a period of time, activity or process
examples: I fell asleep halfway through the movie.
We're about halfway done with the renovation.

senses.head: Informal: partly, or to an acceptable degree
examples: I halfway believed his story.
Anything halfway decent in this neighborhood costs a fortune.

senses.head: In meet someone halfway: to compromise by giving up part of what you want
examples: I can't pay $500, but I'll meet you halfway.
If both sides met halfway, the strike could end tomorrow.

entries.position: mid or end — mid in the degree sense: I halfway believed him
entries.modifies: verbs; adjectives in the degree sense (halfway decent); phrases with through, up, between
entries.form: half + way; older writing has half way or half-way
entries.contrast: For a physical amount English uses half (half empty, half a glass); halfway is for progress through distance or time (halfway home, halfway through the book). Halfway decent is informal for более-менее приличный, not наполовину приличный.
